video_title: Lawfare Daily: Investigating Atrocities in Post-Assad Syria
gist: A commissioner on the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria walks through three post-Assad mass-violence episodes (March 2025 coast, July 2025 Sueda with 1,700 killed and 200,000 displaced, January 2026 against the SDF in the northeast), and argues the al-Shara government is cooperating with its own investigators because it lacks credible domestic legal capacity and needs external legitimation to unlock sanctions relief and investment. She then generalizes to a broader indictment of counterterrorism sanctions as an unmeasured, exceptionalized policy regime that blocked engagement with the very actors now governing Syria, and flags the first-ever break in UN Global Counterterrorism Strategy consensus, with the US, Israel and Argentina voting against.

insights.claim: Syria has seen three major state-directed military campaigns or mass-violence eruptions in roughly thirteen months since the Assad regime fell: coastal violence against the Alawite community in March 2025, the Sueda massacres in July 2025, and state forces moving against Syrian Democratic Forces-held territory in the northeast in January 2026.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: A recurring roughly-every-five-months violence cadence is the base rate anyone underwriting Syrian reconstruction, sanctions relief or regional risk should price, not a series of one-off shocks.

insights.claim: The UN Commission of Inquiry verified 1,700 people killed and over 200,000 forced from their homes in Sueda in July 2025, classifying the conduct as war crimes that may amount to crimes against humanity.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: Hard, government-unchallenged casualty numbers set the factual floor for any future accountability process, reparations claim or conditionality attached to Syrian sanctions relief.

insights.claim: The central risk in post-Assad Syria is not the new government's stated intent but its inability to control coercive forces built out of factions that were themselves designated terrorist groups for the preceding decade and a half.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Command-and-control over integrated ex-militia security forces, not cabinet-level rhetoric, is the variable to monitor for whether Syria stabilizes or repeats sectarian cycles.

insights.claim: The overthrow of the Assad regime involved strikingly little violence relative to the preceding fourteen-year civil war, and the incoming government then exercised security control that almost instantly lowered the temperature of violence nationwide.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: A low-cost transition plus rapid security consolidation is why the downside scenario of state collapse did not materialize; the transition's fragility now runs through episodic communal violence rather than regime instability.
insights.quote: it went out with a whisper and not with a bang

insights.claim: Damascus has normalized enough that a UN commissioner walks around and has coffee in coffee shops there, and during the period when Israel and the United States attacked Iran, Damascus was quite literally the safest place in the Middle East.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: The ground-level security reality in Damascus is running well ahead of Western risk perception, which is exactly the gap that precedes repricing of country risk and first-mover commercial entry.
insights.quote: for Damascus to be the safest place in the Middle East

insights.claim: Normalization in Damascus is not linear: a significant terrorist attack with loss of life occurred in Damascus on the day Emmanuel Macron was visiting, roughly ten days before this conversation.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: High-profile diplomatic visits are attack-attracting events in Syria, a tail risk that can abruptly reverse sentiment and delay sanctions or investment decisions.

insights.claim: A UN special rapporteur and Syria specialist told an international law class in late November 2024 that the Assad regime was going to stay, about a week before the military advances that toppled it, illustrating how badly informed expert consensus mispriced regime durability.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Entrenchment narratives about authoritarian regimes are consistently overweighted right up to collapse; positioning that assumes continuity in sanctioned autocracies carries a fat, unhedged tail.
insights.quote: I think the Assad regime is going to stay

insights.claim: Standing in Damascus airport in July 2023 and seeing scheduled flights to Doha, Tehran and Moscow revealed that Syria was isolated from the West but not from the world, meaning Western sanctions and isolation regimes systematically overstate their own reach.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: A transferable test for any sanctioned economy: check which non-Western routes and centers of power remain open before assuming isolation translates into leverage or into regime fragility.
insights.quote: we the West think that Syria is cut off from the world

themes.theme: Why a new government invites its own indictment

insights.claim: President al-Shara's government deliberately avoided the mass purge the United States carried out in Iraq after toppling Saddam Hussein, so Syria's courts and state structures remain dominated by people affiliated with the former regime and therefore cannot credibly investigate the government's own forces.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Preserved institutional continuity buys stability but creates a durable credibility deficit, which is why external accountability mechanisms remain load-bearing for Syria's international rehabilitation.
insights.quote: So you don't actually have the capacity to do that kind of investigation yourself, at least not in a way that will be viewed as credible, independent, and authoritative by the people of Syria.

insights.claim: The Syrian government granted the Commission of Inquiry access to both the coast and Sueda knowing the findings would implicate its own security forces, did not contest those findings, and accepted the full recommendations, including the finding of war crimes by its own forces.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: Voluntary acceptance of adverse atrocity findings is a rare, observable governance signal that differentiates this government from its predecessor and supports the case for conditional re-engagement.
insights.quote: a marked shift in a conflict that up to that point was simply like nonaccepting of responsibility and non-engagement with accountability in any way

insights.claim: Allowing UN investigators in is a legitimizing move for a government determined to prove it is a rupture from the prior regime, meaning cooperation with atrocity investigations is being used instrumentally as a political asset rather than conceded reluctantly.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: Watch for the moment cooperation stops being useful to the government; the incentive is transactional and could reverse once sanctions relief and recognition are secured.

insights.claim: Physical access to investigate Sueda required two separate negotiations, one with the Syrian state whose forces were under investigation and a second with Druze leadership controlling the ground, morgues and sites of hostilities.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Effective territorial control in Syria is still fragmented between the state and communal authorities, which matters for anyone assessing security, logistics or contract enforcement outside Damascus.

insights.claim: Syrians across Alawite, Druze, Sunni Muslim and Christian communities extend unusual trust to the Commission of Inquiry because it reported on all actors without fear or favor, while the UN's political track lost credibility after repeated failed negotiations that excluded the groups now forming the government.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: Neutrality compounds into an institutional asset that survives regime change, whereas political mediation that picks sides destroys it; the same asymmetry applies to any third-party arbiter in contested markets.
insights.quote: because we reported without fear or favor have an enormous amount of trust

insights.claim: Despite trusting the Commission of Inquiry, most Syrian victims do not believe justice will actually be delivered, because Bashar al-Assad sits in a Moscow suburb having taken a sizable share of the country's fortune with him under the protection of a P5 state.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Great-power protection of a deposed leader caps what accountability mechanisms can deliver, so documentation, not prosecution of principals, is the realistic output to expect from Syria's transitional justice.
insights.quote: many people simply do not believe that justice in its pure sense will be delivered to them

insights.claim: The Syria Commission of Inquiry has operated since 2011 but has shrunk from a peak of almost 30 investigators and forensic experts to just under 10, alongside three geographically diverse commissioners from Brazil, Tunisia and academia.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: Investigative capacity is contracting precisely as post-Assad access finally opens, implying the coverage of future atrocities will be thinner than the historical record suggests.

insights.claim: The commission's database holds over 15,000 testimonies gathered since 2011, and that material has been shared with governments and individual prosecutors and used as the basis for building universal-jurisdiction cases, particularly in Germany and other European states with large Syrian diasporas.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: European universal-jurisdiction prosecutions are a live legal channel driven by UN evidence, creating personal travel and asset risk for individuals implicated in Syrian violence regardless of any domestic amnesty.

insights.claim: The commission works to a civil rather than criminal standard of proof, verifying through survivor interviews, open-source data, satellite imagery and data voluntarily shared by governments, then aggregating incidents into patterns categorized as war crimes, crimes against humanity or genocide.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: Knowing the evidentiary bar is civil, not criminal, tells users how much weight commission findings can carry in courts versus in policy and sanctions decisions.

insights.claim: Trauma fractures memory in ways that make survivors unable to give the linear, fact-based accounts atrocity investigations depend on, so witness-quality degradation is a structural rather than incidental limit on the evidentiary record.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: Documented casualty and violation figures in active conflict zones are systematically lower-bound estimates, which matters when comparing atrocity datasets across conflicts.

insights.claim: In the absence of functioning domestic legal processes, UN fact-finding bodies establish facts that would otherwise be contested by state actors, non-state actors and even victims, and nobody disagreed with the commission's findings on either the coast or Sueda.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: An uncontested factual baseline is the scarce input that lets states, lenders and insurers make Syria decisions at all; commission reports are effectively the reference data for the country.

insights.claim: Rhetorical criticism of the UN coexists with heavy operational reliance on it to establish facts, deliver food and put up tents, and if the UN or the Commission of Inquiry did not exist states would have to invent equivalent bodies after eruptions of violence.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: The gap between anti-UN political rhetoric and actual state dependence suggests multilateral fact-finding functions persist through funding and legitimacy attacks, a durability the headlines understate.
insights.quote: if the UN didn't exist, you'd be inventing it

insights.claim: The global counterterrorism sanctions architecture built from the 1990s al-Qaeda sanctions and extended by post-2001 UN Security Council resolutions has been an utter failure, demonstrated by the fact that in 2026 the people it designated are now running Syria.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: If designation regimes can be invalidated this completely by events, sanctions-driven exclusion of counterparties is a weaker long-term risk signal than compliance frameworks currently assume.
insights.quote: here we are funnily enough 2026 and those people are now running Syria

insights.claim: Terrorist designation is self-defeating because it legally forecloses talking to, negotiating with or engaging the armed actors whose participation is required for de-escalation, ceasefires and conflict-ending sequences, a lesson visible in Northern Ireland as much as Syria.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Designation regimes lengthen conflicts by removing the negotiation option, so the timing of de-listing is a leading indicator of when a conflict can actually be settled.
insights.quote: the fact that they're terrorists means that you can't talk to them

insights.claim: Counterterrorism sanctions have caused humanitarian catastrophe by making it impossible for UN, multilateral and civil society actors to supply food, housing and shelter to civilian populations living in territory controlled by designated groups.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Aid access under designation regimes is a recurring second-order cost that drives displacement, which in turn drives the refugee flows that reshape European domestic politics.

insights.claim: Placing a problem in the counterterrorism box moves it into an exceptional legal and policy regime, and exceptionality has historically insulated itself from the ordinary good-governance assessments applied in every other policy arena.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: A reusable heuristic: any policy domain framed as exceptional escapes effectiveness and value-for-money scrutiny, so its stated efficacy should be discounted by default.
insights.quote: exceptionality has always I think across legal systems and across time in effect insulated itself from the kind of regular business of good governance assessments

insights.claim: If ordinary monitoring and evaluation tests were applied to counterterrorism sanctions, asking whether they ended violence or marginalized target groups, Syria is a classic example where they would literally fail the test.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Framing the critique as a taxpayer value-for-money question rather than a human rights argument is the line most likely to move fiscally conservative policymakers toward de-listing.
insights.quote: they would literally fail the test

insights.claim: States dismantling Syria's multi-tiered sanctions and terrorist designations are recasting them as foreign-relations instruments while pretending their counterterrorism origin story does not exist, avoiding any reckoning with whether those tools ever worked.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Relief granted without acknowledging the tools' failure rests on discretionary political framing rather than reformed criteria, leaving re-designation risk live for anyone entering Syria on the back of it.
insights.quote: pretending that the roots of these kinds of tools are not in fact and and ultimately are counterterrorism tools

themes.theme: US self-isolation at the UN counterterrorism vote

insights.claim: The UN Global Counterterrorism Strategy, adopted in 2006 and renewed by consensus at every cycle since, was passed by a divided vote for the first time this year, with the United States, Israel and Argentina voting against it.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: The breaking of a twenty-year consensus in one of the few areas where P5 and small states always agreed is a concrete marker of multilateral fragmentation in global security.
insights.quote: the outliers to the consensus were the United States, Israel, and Argentina

insights.claim: The United States offered a late, hastily drafted alternative counterterrorism strategy that stripped out two decades of accumulated human rights and rule-of-law standards, and the vast majority of states rejected it in favor of the negotiated text.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: US drafting power at the UN no longer converts into outcomes even in a domain it defined after 9/11, which lowers the expected value of unilateral US pressure in multilateral security forums.

insights.claim: The Europeans, Russians and Chinese all stayed inside the counterterrorism consensus and will continue cooperating in that space while the United States sits outside it, reflecting an American rejection of compromise as a defining virtue of global action.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Cooperation continuing without the US means intelligence, listing and operational coordination norms will be set by others, an erosion of influence that compounds quietly rather than visibly.
insights.quote: We don't want to do this with you anymore. We are going to disagree.

insights.claim: Spoiler politics offers momentary pleasure but strategic allies and adversaries play a long game, so the short-termism of the current US approach to international law limits the range of options and partners available and carries infinite, undercalibrated long-term security costs.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: The cost of outcasting shows up with a lag in coalition availability and burden-sharing, not immediately, which is precisely why it is systematically underpriced in current policy.
insights.quote: the dangers of that to the long-term security of the United States are infinite and of course undercalibrated by this administration

themes.theme: Rule-of-law conditionality as the Syria trade

insights.claim: The explicit recommendation to states weighing sanctions relief, investment and security agreements with Syria is to bet on Syria but bet on the rule of law in Syria, because security guarantees such as joining the global coalition against Daesh will be worth nothing without parallel investment in governance.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Frames the Syria opportunity as conditional and governance-linked rather than a straight reopening trade, and identifies rule-of-law progress as the variable to track before committing capital.
insights.quote: you have to bet on Syria, but bet on the rule of law in Syria

insights.claim: The US government wrote the Commission of Inquiry into the Sueda roadmap because when domestic legal systems do not function the international community wants an insurance policy on what is happening inside a country it is deciding whether to support economically, politically and diplomatically.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
insights.so_what: Commission reporting functions as the de facto gating indicator for Syrian sanctions relief and official finance, so its publication calendar is a tradeable event schedule for Syria exposure.
insights.quote: the international community wants an insurance policy on what's happening inside a country

insights.claim: Fourteen years of competing external intervention in Syria by the United States, Russia, Iran, Turkey and the European Union produced a zero-sum outcome in which the states' bets, including the bet that Assad would survive, cancelled each other out, and Sudan is now a prime example of the same folly repeating.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Multi-party proxy backing tends to neutralize itself and extend conflicts, which argues for pricing longer duration into any conflict with three or more external sponsors, Sudan included.
insights.quote: the continued bet on different parties including a bet that Assad would survive

insights.claim: Failing to engage the causes of conflict means the cost is absorbed domestically instead, as Syria's war produced the largest refugee flows in recent memory into Lebanon, Jordan, Germany and other European states, with all the downstream domestic consequences that followed in Europe.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Links conflict-resolution underinvestment directly to European migration politics, implying that European stakes in Syrian stabilization are domestic rather than merely humanitarian and support sustained European engagement.
insights.quote: when you don't actually engage to address the causes of conflict, you absorb the cost of that conflict domestically

insights.claim: Twenty years of experience since 9/11 and the Iraq war show that counterterrorism without effective investment in the social conditions that produce violence undoes all the counterterrorism work, making it both a poor bet and a poor spend.
insights.speaker: guest, UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria commissioner
insights.so_what: Provides the causal argument for why security-only packages in Syria should be expected to fail, and why development and governance spending is the complement that determines whether the security spend holds.
insights.quote: counterterrorism without effective investment in the things that produce violence in society undoes all of your counterterrorism work

top_entities: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria
